Sources indicate that every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them. Asking questions about medical care is perfectly reasonable (in fact, informed pet parents should!), but dismissing vaccination without understanding the risks is another story.

Rabies is a perfect example. This is not some historical disease or something that only affects animals in remote areas or underdeveloped countries. It can infect mammals, including our own cats, dogs, and even us. Whatâs even scarier is that once the clinical signs appear, rabies is almost always fatal, making prevention essential.

Recent events in Quebec offer a timely reminder. Amid an emerging wildlife outbreak, three domestic cats tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies in 2026. Although these numbers pale in comparison to the number of infected wildlife recorded since December 20241, it demonstrates how a disease circulating in wild animals can reach our pets.

Sources indicate that and this isn't just a Canadian concern. Rabies variants and wildlife risks differ by region, but keeping pets appropriately vaccinated is a responsibility shared by pet parents everywhere.

Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

Rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. Since then, more outbreaks have appeared, and case numbers have climbed sharply in 2026, particularly in MontÃ©rÃ©gie. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. The three infected cats are examples of how a virus circulating in wildlife can also reach our pets, even though cats are not the main reservoir responsible for spreading this variant.

In a recent development, cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very rapidly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. A skunk hiding beneath a shed may be investigated by a curious feline. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. And cats being cats, curiosity can get them into trouble! These encounters don't just happen deep in the woods. A backyard, garage, or garden fence can be enough.

According to recent reports, one of the infected cats was believed to have contracted rabies after contact with a wild animal. Another case led to three people receiving preventive treatment following possible exposure.

In a recent development, rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so crucial.

When people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

Recent findings suggest that in cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. A normally friendly kitty may suddenly become grumpy, hide more than usual, vocalize differently, lose interest in food, or behave in ways that seem completely out of character. Since cats are already experts at keeping their humans guessing, a sudden behavior change can sometimes be easy to dismiss. But when a cat starts acting noticeably different from their usual, wonderfully weird self, it's worth paying attention.

As the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

Industry observers note that there is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. So no, a rabid animal doesn't necessarily look like it's auditioning for a horror movie.

Of course, these signs can also occur with other neurological conditions, injuries, and intoxications. Nobody should attempt to diagnose rabies based on behavior alone. A cat showing sudden, unexplained neurological changes needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if wildlife exposure is possible.

Here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. A cat may seem perfectly fine after an encounter with an infected animal, but that doesn't mean the virus isn't already in its body. So if a possible exposure happens, don't wait for your cat to look sick before calling the vet. By then, it may be too late.

According to recent reports, sadly, once rabies reaches the clinical stage, there is no cure, and the outcome is almost always fatal. That's why a suspected exposure should never be a wait-and-see situation. Don't wait for signs to appear; contact your veterinarian right away. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

Sources indicate that think your indoor cat doesn't need a rabies vaccine? Think again! Indoor cats have fewer opportunities to encounter wildlife, but escapes happen, doors get left open, and sometimes wildlife finds its way indoors. Nobody aims these little adventures, least of all the cat!

Rabies vaccination is also required by law for cats in many countries and jurisdictions. Even where it isn't mandatory, keeping your cat vaccinated is an vital part of preventive care. Ask your veterinarian about the appropriate schedule for your cat.

Sources indicate that and remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

In a recent development, if your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

Recent findings suggest that keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

Recent findings suggest that if a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

And please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

Sources indicate that quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

Recent findings suggest that cats will be cats. A rustling bush can become the most fascinating thing in the universe, and a passing raccoon may look like an invitation to investigate. We can't blame them for being curious. We can give them safer ways to enjoy their adventures.

#32966. These 8 Evergreen Plants Make Your Porch Look Magical at Christmas – And They Stay Gorgeous All Winter

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1724 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

These 8 Evergreen Plants Make Your Porch Look Magical at Christmas – And They Stay Gorgeous All Winter

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight.
  • Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter.
  • According to recent reports, best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight. Yet when chosen thoughtfully, they can become show-stopping centerpieces. This is a time of year to celebrate the holiday season, but rather than relying on temporary displays, why not go for something with real staying power?

Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter. Flanking a front door or framing porch steps with holiday porch pots filled with living potted evergreens offers charm and longevity. Beyond classic deep emerald needles, today’s best container evergreens can deliver winter berries, flowers, contrasting textures, and even fragrance to greet guests as they arrive at your stoop.

According to recent reports, best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down. With minimal upkeep, they lend easy elegance through the dark days of winter, then you can move them as needed to assist in decades-long displays. From trailing options to compact shrubs, here are 8 gorgeous evergreens you can use to transform your front porch into an enchanting holiday welcome.

Recent findings suggest that growing evergreens in containers unlocks wonderful design flexibility, allowing you to cluster different heights, trailing textures, and berry accents right at eye level near your doorway. However, while container-grown evergreens are generally easygoing and make great seasonal décor, they need a little more winter care than evergreens growing in the ground.

In a recent development, because their potted roots sit above ground, they are more vulnerable to freezing temperatures and drying winter winds. It’s a good idea to choose evergreen varieties that are rated at least one or two USDA hardiness zones colder than your local climate, so plant roots have the best shot at surviving winter freezes unscathed.

Use frost-proof containers crafted from thick resin, fiberglass, glazed stoneware, or heavy wood. Avoid unglazed thin terracotta in cold climates, as trapped moisture will expand and crack clay walls. If your winters are very cold, consider wrapping the pots in burlap. Always leave unobstructed drainage holes and elevate your pots slightly on pot feet so icy water doesn't have a chance to pool underneath. You can buy Tortoise Pot Toes from Amazon to help ensure the best drainage.

In a recent development, fill the containers with a coarse, fast-draining potting mix. Once you are past the holiday season and heading to spring, you can add a slow-release organic fertilizer. Even in winter, evergreens continue losing moisture through their foliage. Check the soil every couple of weeks and water deeply whenever the top two inches (5cm) feel dry and temperatures are above freezing. You’re now ready to add some of these evergreens to make your porch sparkle during Christmas and shine all winter long….

Sources indicate that alberta spruce is a classic choice for a Christmas tree, but most are large. If you fancy flanking your front door with classic, miniature Christmas trees, dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca ‘Conica’) is perfect for a pot. Hardy across zones 3-8, this conifer naturally grows into a dense, velvety green, symmetrical cone, so it requires zero shearing to maintain its crisp silhouette. Also, because it adds just 2-4 inches (5-10cm) of growth per year, it thrives in a generous 14-18-inch (35-45cm) container for years, before needing upsizing or transplanting into the yard.

Recent findings suggest that place in full sun to light afternoon shade, rotating every few weeks. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but sharply drained, and mist occasionally. For a little extra holiday magic, underplant with trailing wintergreen or variegated ivy. Avoid heavy ornaments that might bend the fine branch tips. You can buy Dwarf Alberta Spruce from Nature Hills at a 30% discount. Add a couple for a lovely, symmetrical entryway feature.

Recent findings suggest that boxwood (Buxus spp.) brings classic English-garden elegance to winter porches in zones 5-9. Its dense clusters of small, glossy leaves stay green through sub-freezing weather. For containers, choose compact, cold-hardy cultivars such as Green Velvet (which forms a lush, rounded mound) or Green Gem. You can buy Brighter Blooms Green Velvet Boxwood from Walmart. Alternatively, go for pre-trained pyramid and globe topiaries for instant architectural polish.

Sources indicate that place potted boxwoods in partial shade to full sun. In northern zones, shelter them from harsh afternoon winter sun and drying winds. Plant in well-drained potting soil, and water deeply when unfrozen soil dries out. Dress for the holidays with velvet ribbon bows or tuck crimson winterberry stems into the soil around the base. Save any light shaping shears for late spring after the risk of last frost is passed.

In a recent development, nothing reveals the arrival of Christmas quite like holly (Ilex spp.), with its glossy leaves and scarlet berries. While towering tree hollies quickly outgrow porch pots, compact shrub cultivars thrive in containers in zones 5-9. Look for dwarf selections such as Little Red or compact Japanese Helleri. Alternatively, try deciduous winterberry Berry Poppins. Buy Proven Winners Berry Poppins Winterberry Holly from Plant Addicts for a container-sized beauty loaded with vibrant berry clusters.

Just remember that hollies are dioecious. To enjoy berries, you need a female cultivar paired near a compatible male (such as Mr Poppins for winterberry). Failing that, buy a nursery pot where both sexes are planted together. Grow hollies in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic potting mix. Keep berries safely out of reach of pets, and enjoy watching winter songbirds visit as spring approaches.

If your front porch sits beneath a deep overhang or faces north where sun-loving conifers struggle, Japanese skimmia (Skimmia japonica) is a revelation. Hardy in zones 6-8, this neat, mounded broadleaf evergreen thrives in partial to full shade, retaining leathery, aromatic leaves all year. Better still, it delivers multi-season magic: in fall and early winter, male cultivars like Rubella produce clusters of flower buds that last right through Christmas, before opening into fragrant spring blossoms, while female varieties like Reevesiana bear true red berries.

Industry observers note that plant skimmia in an acidic, humus-rich potting mix (such as an ericaceous blend) with sharp drainage. Water regularly during dry spells, using rainwater if your tap water is hard. Nestle pots in a sheltered porch corner that is protected from icy gales. You can buy Skimmia Male Plants from Plant Addicts for shade-loving beauty to bedazzle on a covered porch. Add pinecones and ribbons to make pots festive.

Also known as eastern teaberry or boxberry, American wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens) is a low-growing native evergreen groundcover. But it punches above its compact 6-inch (15cm) height in winter containers. Hardy in zones 3-8, its shiny, oval leaves transform over winter, from deep green to mahogany-bronze in cold weather. This provides a gorgeous backdrop for large, glossy red berries that cling to the stems all winter long.

Because it trails gracefully over pot rims, it makes a lovely festive spiller around the base of dwarf spruce, boxwood, or winterberry stems in mixed holiday planters. Give it a spot in partial to full shade. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic potting soil. Keep soil consistently damp and avoid lime-heavy fertilizers. You can buy Arbor Day Foundation Store’s Wintergreen Teaberry Pot Plants from Amazon in triple packs. Perfect under a porch cover, awning, or larger tree or shrub.

Industry observers note that goldcrest cypress aka Goldcrest Monterey cypress (Hesperocyparis macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) is also sold as lemon cypress, and it lives up to its names in winter porches. Hardy in zones 7-10 (and also enjoyed as a cool-room or sheltered patio container specimen in colder zones), this upright conifer is filled with chartreuse-gold foliage that releases a zesty aroma when you brush past it. You can buy Wonderland Flora’s Lemon Cypress Goldcrest Wilma Plants from Walmart in packs of four.

According to recent reports, its narrow, columnar shape fits neatly into tight entryway corners and pairs symmetrically beside front doors. Grow Goldcrest in full sun to intensify its golden hues, and plant in a fast-draining potting mix. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, but don’t let roots sit in soggy saucers. Dress the pot base with pinecones and burgundy ribbon for a contemporary holiday look that keeps sparkling into spring.

If you need to soften the edges of a structured winter pot, add some cascading English ivy (Hedera helix). Hardy in zones 4-9, this classic vining evergreen offers lobed emerald or crisp cream-and-gold variegations. Try cultivars like Glacier and Goldchild to brighten shady entryways with ease. While it can be invasive in the ground, it thrives in containers. Plant around the lip of mixed planters with upright boxwood or red-berried skimmia, or train up a wire obelisk for vertical interest.

Ivy thrives in partial to full shade, and prefers slightly drier, well-drained potting soil. Overwatering in winter is the main enemy. Just snip stray runners occasionally to keep trails tidy, and never allow stems to root into surrounding masonry. You can buy Glacier Ivy from Plant Addicts for trailing creams and greens to add lush, lively winter movement.

It has been revealed that if you want guests to pause in delight at your front door, plant sweet box (Sarcococca confusa). Hardy in zones 6-9, this understated, slow-growing broadleaf evergreen features dense, pointed leaves that look refined all year. What makes it unique for holiday decorating is that it flowers in winter. Depending on where you garden, you’ll have either buds or open flowers on this evergreen shrub at Christmas time. As a bonus, these creamy flowers are sweetly fragrant even on chilly days.

Sweet box thrives in deep to partial shade and prefers shelter from winds, so a covered front porch or courtyard alcove is ideal. Plant in a medium-sized container filled with rich, well-drained, neutral-to-slightly-acidic potting mix. Keep soil evenly moist when unfrozen. Minimal pruning is required: simply snip a few fragrant sprigs to tuck into holiday vases. You can buy Hirt’s Gardens Sweet & Lo Sweet Box Plants from Amazon for a shade-loving evergreen that fills entryways with honey scent.

48 Bulldogs, One Apartment, and a Disturbing Secret

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dogster

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you.
  • Forty-eight dogs â mostly French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs â found in what authorities are describing as a clandestine breeding operation in San Juan de Miraflores, Peru.
  • And when you read what was found, it is hard not to feel angry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

This is exactly why we are against puppy mills.

Forty-eight dogs â mostly French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs â found in what authorities are describing as a clandestine breeding operation in San Juan de Miraflores, Peru.

And when you read what was found, it is hard not to feel angry.

In a recent development, authorities discovered the animals in appalling conditions on September 28 in an apartment on JirÃ³n Santiago RodrÃ­guez. The group included 25 French Bulldogs, nine English Bulldogs, eight mixed-breed dogs, five French Bulldog puppies, and one Dachshund. There was also a rooster. Local French Bulldog club, Club Frenchie, heard about the rescue through social media and immediately reached out to offer assistance. One member of the club spoke to a reporter from the Peruvian newspaper El Comercio about what they had witnessed:.

According to recent reports, âThe state of health was absolutely deplorable. There were dogs covered in feces, filthy, with no hygiene whatsoever, dogs with broken nails, bitten ears, and other serious problems,â he mentioned.

The dogs were brought to the Municipal Veterinary Clinic in San Juan de Miraflores, where they were examined and received treatment for a range of conditions. Most were suffering from heat stress, and many had excessively long nails, some bleeding, skin problems, fungal issues, eye infections, surgical scars, and other conditions requiring medical attention. Six puppies reportedly needed incubator care, with two described as being in a particularly fragile condition.

Following the intervention, the animals were taken to the municipal veterinary service, and some have since been moved into foster care. The San Juan de Miraflores Provincial Corporate Criminal Prosecutor's Office is investigating the case, and FÃ©lix Sonco and Darlys Vanegas were arrested at the scene.

As if the horrendous conditions that greeted rescuers werenât disturbing enough, it appears that this wasnât simply a breeding operation, but an illegal, makeshift veterinary clinic.

Some of these dogs had undergone surgery on their vocal cords; a barbaric procedure known as debarking. Being kept in cramped and filthy conditions meant that these dogs were barking and crying constantly. Debarking was a way to reduce noise and avoid complaints.

They didnât improve conditions. They didnât provide relief. They simply removed their ability to voice their distress.

Evidence also suggests that several female Bulldogs were bred repeatedly, with some reportedly forced to carry as many as ten litters of puppies. Veterinary examination also found evidence that crude cesarean surgeries had been performed prematurely to get puppies out faster and back on the market, while the mothers, if they survived, were bred again.

Investigators reportedly found premature newborn puppies inside an unsterilized incubator, while puppies were being sold for around 1,500 to 2,500 Peruvian soles each â roughly $400 to $670 USD.

In a recent development, french Bulldogs and English Bulldogs are brachycephalic breeds. Their shortened skull and squishy faces are a big part of their appeal. But there is a very uncomfortable truth behind that cute face.

That same anatomy that many people find irresistible can make it harder for a dog to breathe, exercise, sleep, regulate their body temperature, and, in some cases, give birth.

We have to stop pretending these things are simply âpart of being a Bulldog.â.

Recent findings suggest that A dog struggling to breathe is not just a snorer. A dog that overheats easily is not just âsensitive to the heat.â These are medical problems.

Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) refers to the conditions that affect breeds with a shortened skull, or âbrachycephaly.â These conditions include hypoplastic trachea (narrow  windpipe), stenotic nares (narrow nostrils), and a tongue and soft palate that are too large and long for the mouth, resulting in obstruction of the airways and difficulty swallowing.

Recent findings suggest that these issues have led many veterinary professionals and animal welfare advocates to question the ethics of breeding these dogs. When a physical characteristic can affect basic functions like breathing and temperature regulation, choosing which dogs reproduce needs to consider more than appearance.

Recent findings suggest that that little flat face. Those massive eyes. The stout little body. The funny little snorts.

In a recent development, most people see cute, even adorable. But as veterinarians, we see a whole list of problems that need to be monitored.

Industry observers note that A Bulldog can be an absolutely wonderful companion and still have anatomy that puts them at risk for serious health problems. Breeding of these dogs should require more responsibility, not less, with breeders selecting for less extreme conformations.

There is something very sad about how much importance we place on how dogs look. A certain face. A certain size. A certain coat. A certain breed.

The more desirable that look becomes, the more money there is in producing it. That creates a market, and unfortunately, where there is money, there will always be those willing to cut corners.

In a recent development, this does not mean that every breeder is bad. There are responsible breeders who health-test their dogs, carefully select breeding pairs, provide appropriate veterinary care, and take responsibility for the puppies they bring into the world. Those who are actively trying to breed healthier versions of dogs whose health and function have been crippled through selective breeding for exaggerated features.

Puppy mills are something very different.

The problem is when the animals producing those puppies become a means to an end.

A female dog becomes a breeding machine.

And veterinary care becomes an expense to minimize or avoid, not an essential part of responsible animal care.

It has been revealed that when it comes to looking for your next four-legged family member, start your search at an animal shelter. Research your favorite breed and know how to recognize a suspicious situation.

If you are planning to purchase or adopt a puppy, you should be able to inspect the home or facility where the puppy was raised, and meet the puppyâs mother. Breeders who are unwilling or unable to allow this raise suspicions of unethical practice, and if you are concerned about a potential welfare glitch, donât be tempted to buy a puppy to ârescueâ it â this simply finances the operation. Instead, contact your local animal control agency, humane society, sheriff, or police department.

Sources indicate that when extreme conformation interferes with breathing and thermoregulation, when it increases the risk of difficult births and chronic airway problems, we need to consider whether breeding these dogs is the right thing to do. But if people will buy them, people will breed them.

Itâs up to us to look past the adorable face we saw on Instagram and ask:.

Are they breathing comfortably?

Do they have functional airways?

And, as the horrific plight of these 48 dogs reminds us, where did they come from?

Loving Bulldogs is not the problem.

The problem is loving an appearance so much that we stop asking what that appearance means for the animal.

These dogs have been through a terrible situation, but now they have a chance.

According to recent reports, they need veterinary care. Their nails need treatment, their skin and eyes need evaluation, their nutritional needs need to be addressed, and their other medical problems need to be properly investigated. Some require specialized treatment, while others are recovering in foster homes.

And hopefully, many of these dogs will eventually experience something that should have been completely ordinary from the beginning:.

These dogs were not born to produce puppies. They were not born to be quiet. They were not born to look a certain way for someone else's profit.

For that reason, adoption should always be considered before buying a puppy.

Sources indicate that there are so many wonderful dogs already waiting in shelters, foster homes, and recovering from neglect. Dogs that may not have the perfect face or pedigree but have an enormous capacity to love.

They don't need to be produced.

Please, before asking where to buy the puppy with the cutest face, ask who is already waiting for someone to choose them.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way.
  • Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

Lowering the risk: Genetics play a substantial part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which shows up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

According to recent reports, lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

Lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

It has been revealed that this is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight rapidly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

Up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

According to recent reports, lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

In a recent development, rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

It has been revealed that lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

According to recent reports, lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a blueprint for each cat.

Dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

In a recent development, dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

Recent findings suggest that the key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

Industry observers note that naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

Industry observers note that boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

Industry observers note that A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Sources indicate that ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

In a recent development, dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

Feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

Loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

In a recent development, different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

In a recent development, training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

It has been revealed that create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

According to recent reports, avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

In a recent development, for dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying issue rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December. The water behind it has nowhere to go. Once nights stay below 32°F (0°C), it can freeze solid, and copper and brass don't have much give. Something splits. That repair bill usually runs well past what the faucet cost, so it pays to sort out how to winterize an outdoor faucet now.

It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers. The annoying part is where the damage hides. From the yard, the faucet can look fine while the pipe behind it has cracked a few inches inside the wall. Nobody sees that until the water's back on.

Outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again. Take off the hose, shut off the supply, drain what's left, and add a cover for backup. Try to finish alongside your other gardening winterizing tasks, and before the first hard freeze indicates up in the forecast.

If you only get to one step today, make it this one. Any hose left on the spigot holds water inside the faucet, and that goes for frost-free models too – the water has nowhere to drain while the hose is attached. Splitters, watering timers, and quick-connect fittings trap water the same way, so pull them all off.

Then empty the hose. Stretch it down a slope or drape loops over a fence rail so the water runs out both ends. Leftover water can freeze and split it, and a drained hose stored out of the weather generally holds up longer. Suncast's 100-foot Hose Hideaway from Walmart keeps a coiled hose off the ground under a lid.

It has been revealed that start inside. Standard faucets usually have their own shutoff, somewhere close to where the pipe goes out through the wall, often in a basement, crawl space, or utility room. Look up between the ceiling joists, too. A round handle turns clockwise until it stops. If it's a lever, a quarter turn puts it crosswise to the pipe, and that's closed.

According to recent reports, not every home has one, and older houses often don't, which makes it harder to winterize hose bib lines without shutting off water to the whole house. If you're not sure what an unlabeled valve is, leave it alone. Close the wrong one, and it's no fun to find out halfway through washing dishes. Frost-free faucets, like this SharkBite one, work differently and may not need this step.

For faucets without a dedicated indoor shutoff, a Freeze Miser outdoor faucet protector offers another option. It screws onto the spigot and automatically releases a small amount of water when the water temperature drops below 37°F (3°C), helping prevent freezing. Unlike conventional winterizing, this method requires leaving the water supply on and the outdoor faucet fully open.

Industry observers note that head back outside and open the faucet all the way. Some water should run out, slow to a trickle, and stop. Did it keep flowing? Then the indoor valve isn't closed all the way, or it's not the right valve at all.

According to recent reports, some shutoffs have a little cap on the side, called a bleeder. Leave the outdoor faucet open so air can get in, set a bucket underneath, and back the cap off slowly. Water will dribble out. When it quits, screw the cap back on. Many plumbers will leave the outdoor faucet open all winter. Some valve makers say to close it, though, so go by whatever came with yours.

Recent findings suggest that an outdoor faucet cover holds in a little of the warmth that seeps through the wall from inside. The rigid type (like the image above) is a foam-lined dome with a cord that pulls it snug against the siding. Home Depot's Everbilt hard outdoor faucet cover is a good cheap option. Flexible pouches go on more like a sock (see image below), and the Thinsulate-lined faucet socks on Amazon come two to a pack.

Either kind should sit flat against the wall with no gap for cold air. Check it after windy nights, because covers do get knocked loose. It's backup, not a substitute for unhooking hoses and draining the line, and outdoor spigot winter protection still starts with an empty faucet. An Ambient Weather Wi-Fi weather station can send temperature alerts to your phone before a hard freeze.

Plenty of people hear frost-free and figure that means forget about it. That's about half right, maybe. From the yard, a frost-free outdoor faucet looks like any other spigot. Its handle turns a long stem, and the part that stops the water sits way back at the end of it, where it's warmer. Close it, and the water in that stem should run out the spout. That only works if the faucet slopes a little toward the outside.

So the hose still comes off, or water stays put and can freeze inside the wall, often unnoticed until spring. Damage, a level installation, or a pipe running through an unheated crawl space can leave one vulnerable too.

Industry observers note that correctly installed ones usually don't need the supply shut off and drained, but the manufacturer's instructions get the final say. Homes without an indoor shutoff can have a plumber fit a replacement such as the SharkBite one mentioned above.

In a recent development, if the faucet won't run or ice has formed around the spout, skip the torch, even if one happens to be sitting right there in the garage. No open flame, and nothing else that blasts heat at it, either. There's framing and insulation right behind that siding. Hair dryers are slower. Point it at the faucet and the wall around it and give it time. Keep the cord out of puddles.

Suspect a leak? Shut off the water to that line, or the main valve if there's no separate one, and call a plumber. Frozen pipe damage isn't always visible right away. A crack of ⅛ inch (3 mm) can let out up to 250 gallons (946L) a day, and it may not drip at all until the ice thaws or the water goes back on.

Most of what it takes to protect outdoor faucets from freezing – and to prevent frozen pipes behind them – is getting the water out and keeping it out. Get that done before the first hard frost, and the faucet should be ready come spring, with dry walls behind it.

Something vital to understand about shelter dogs is that a kennel is an extremely specific, highly stressful environment. A dog may be overwhelmed, overstimulated, shut down, or frustrated by everything happening around them. Rightfully so â they don't understand why they're there.

Shelter staff and volunteers who care for these animals daily see glimpses of their true nature, but an adopter on the other side of the kennel door rarely sees beyond the first impression.

Not every dog has an immediate foster match; some need a very specific environment, routine, or space. When those resources aren't available, dogs can remain in shelters for months. And the longer they wait, the easier it can be for people to overlook them. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Poinsettias might be the traditional choice for festive decorating, but they're not the only Christmas houseplants capable of bringing a splash of holiday color indoors.

According to recent reports, if you're looking for something a little different this year, there is a holiday plant that promises the same bold red hues of a poinsettia, along with glossy succulent leaves and a surprisingly easygoing nature. And no, we're not talking about sweet box (although that's also a brilliant container plant to add to your shopping list).

Instead, we're dragging the beautiful Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) into the spotlight, as its flowers can last for weeks, making it a lovely way to brighten your home through the darker months.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Often sold as a seasonal flowering plant, Flaming Katy is actually a tender perennial succulent, which means you don't necessarily have to throw it away once Christmas is over. In fact, all you have to do is give it the right conditions and it can continue growing for years, potentially rewarding you with another spectacular display.

In a recent development, there's no denying that poinsettias look impressive, but they can be surprisingly fussy about their surroundings, as they dislike cold draughts and sudden temperature changes – so much so that their leaves can drop. Overwatering is another common problem, particularly when plants are left sitting in decorative pots without adequate drainage.

Sources indicate that flaming Katy offers a much easier alternative, as its leaves store water, helping it cope with occasional dry spells, while its clusters of brightly colored flowers provide plenty of festive impact. Red is a particularly popular choice for Christmas, of course, although you can also find varieties with pink, orange, yellow and white flowers, too.

According to recent reports, better still? Rather than providing a brief burst of colour, a healthy plant can remain in bloom for several weeks, sometimes even longer depending on the variety and growing conditions.

Unlike some Christmas houseplants, this one doesn't need constant attention to keep looking good. Once you find a suitable position (a birght windowsill is ideal), the main thing is to avoid overwatering and make sure it receives enough light.

It also prefers average indoor humidity, so there's no need to mist it or create a particularly humid environment; in fact, good air circulation is more useful than excessive moisture around the leaves. Just keep it somewhere warm, ideally with temperatures around 60–75°F (16–24°C), and give it plenty of bright, indirect light (and remember that some gentle morning sunshine is generally welcome, too).

During the flowering period, you can remove individual faded flower clusters to keep the plant looking tidy, but there's no need for complicated pruning or constant feeding.

Perhaps the best thing about Flaming Katy is that, even though it's a Christmas houseplant, it doesn't have to be a disposable festive decoration; once flowering finishes, you can continue growing it as a foliage houseplant. With the right care, it can produce new growth and flower again.

Recent findings suggest that oh sure, poinsettias will always have their place in Christmas decorating, but Flaming Katy makes a convincing alternative if you'd prefer something colorful, undemanding and potentially longer-lasting when it comes to brightening up a home during winter. And unlike a certain fussy red plant that pops up everywhere in the holidays, this little flowering succulent really can stick around for years.

    Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their dog's health and well-being.

    Industry observers note that whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned dog lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your furry friend happy and healthy. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

    It has been revealed that âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

    According to recent reports, when my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

    Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

    Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

    According to recent reports, you have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

    It has been revealed that I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

    It has been revealed that please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

    Sources indicate that I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical challenges sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

    He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

    Industry observers note that that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is at the moment looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

    This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

    It has been revealed that TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

    According to recent reports, rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

    In a recent development, the interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

    Recent findings suggest that the Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

    For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

    Lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

    Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

    TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

    It has been revealed that the current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

    Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

    Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

    Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

    For families who decide to participate, it is important to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

    When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

    The recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

    According to recent reports, there's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a major deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

    But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

    Industry observers note that aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

    The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

    Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

    According to recent reports, the Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

    Itâs crucial to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

    When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

    And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

    In a recent development, that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

    For owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

    So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

    Recent findings suggest that halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

    Industry observers note that keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

    Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs vital to pay attention to how they respond.

    Sources indicate that A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

    Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

    Sources indicate that A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

    There's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

    Industry observers note that halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

    Sources indicate that A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

    Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

    Jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

    Real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

    Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

    The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

    Recent findings suggest that check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

    Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

    Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

    Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

    An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly important on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

    Recent findings suggest that if a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

    Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

    According to recent reports, halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

    It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

    #32942. What Your Jade Plant Needs in November – 5 Easy Ways to Unlock Lush Growth and Good Fortune in the New Year
