    According to recent reports, robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse are fast becoming the it couple of the moment (not least of all because the man formerly known as Edward Cullen is now Bond, James Bond). So you'd best believe they're setting trends left, right, and center – even in the world of indoor gardening.

    According to recent reports, and while we'd expect the pair to have a suitably impressive garden, it turns out their houseplant of choice is considerably more interesting than your average monstera or spider plant. In fact, it's a miniature tree with a rather sophisticated reputation: the not-so-humble bonsai!

    Yes, with the couple's busy schedules taking them between different homes and locations, it makes sense that they're all about the idea of bringing greenery indoors. After all, houseplants offer a lovely way to make a space feel personal, even when you're not necessarily putting down roots for the long term. And if you're going to invest in an indoor plant, then why not make it something a little more unusual?

    Speaking to the Perfectly Imperfect Newsletter in September 2024, Suki Waterhouse revealed that she developed a rather unexpected obsession with bonsai trees during the final month of her pregnancy.

    According to recent reports, 'When I was preggers in the last month and didn’t really feel like seeing anyone, I got obsessed with getting a bonsai tree,' she says. 'I found a number on Google and pulled up to a house in East Hollywood and a lady had a bunch of them locked up in her back garden. Felt super cool and mysterious. Some of them she’d had for 30 years. Fell in love with this guy and have become obsessed with pruning.'.

    The leaves on this bonsai fold up at night or in subdued light, and it wakes up when we do!

    Industry observers note that it's a wonderfully specific plant obsession, and one we can absolutely get behind. Especially as there's something rather magical about a tiny tree that's been carefully cultivated for decade; there's a reason that bonsai is as much an art form as it is a gardening hobby.

    Of course, Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson aren't the only ones who appreciate the appeal of the beautiful bonsai tree. In fact, there's been something of a growing appreciation for the slower, more mindful side of gardening, and bonsai? Why, that fits the philosophy rather beautifully.

    Recent findings suggest that more importantly? Well, despite the fact that bonsai trees have a reputation for being (whisper it) high-maintenance, they're not as intimidating as their appearance might suggest. The trick is choosing the right one – so look for a variety suited to indoor conditions and make a note of its basic requirements. And, as Suki herself pointed out, a little regular pruning and thoughtful watering can go a long way.

    If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have inspired you to introduce a little bonsai magic into your own home, there are a few varieties worth considering...

    In a recent development, if you're newly introduced to bonsai, ficus is arguably the best place to start. These tropical trees are considerably more forgiving than many traditional bonsai varieties and adapt well to indoor conditions. Their glossy leaves and interesting roots make them particularly striking, too.

    Give something like this Small Ficus Live Bonsai Tree from Brussell's Bonsai a bright position with plenty of indirect light, keep it away from cold draughts and water when the top layer of compost begins to dry.

    If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have got you in the mood for something a little more unusual, consider the Hawaiian umbrella tree (Schefflera arboricola).

    This bonsai's distinctive leaves and naturally branching growth make it a particularly attractive choice for an indoor plant.

    It has been revealed that it's also relatively tolerant of indoor humidity levels and can cope with slightly less-than-perfect light conditions, although a bright spot will always help it thrive. Take care to allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and prune regularly to maintain its shape.

    A lovely option for anyone who tends to be a little forgetful with watering, jade bonsai (Crassula ovata) is a succulent that enjoys plenty of bright light and needs much less frequent watering than tropical bonsai varieties.

    Pick up something like this Live Jade from Brussell's Bonsai, let the compost dry out thoroughly between waterings, and make sure it's planted in a free-draining bonsai mix to prevent its roots from sitting in excess moisture.

    Of course, even the most beginner-friendly bonsai isn't quite a plant you can forget about. Even Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse will tell you, light, watering and occasional pruning are all key, and it's worth remembering that not every bonsai is suited to indoor living.

    As a general rule of thumb, tropical and subtropical varieties are generally the best choice for growing inside; most traditional temperate trees need to experience the changing seasons outdoors.

    Recent findings suggest that still, there's something rather lovely about the idea of tending to a little tree that could stay with you for decades. And if Suki Waterhouse's experience is anything to go by, it might just become your next very absorbing, very cool, very mysterious hobby.

    • It has been revealed that it’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

    It has been revealed that it’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

    It has been revealed that with 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

    In a recent development, some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

    Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis.

    Industry observers note that conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

    According to recent reports, finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

    Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

    Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

    Sources indicate that another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

    Patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, latest pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is important to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

    Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

    Recent findings suggest that repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

    Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

    I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

    According to recent reports, it’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

    Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

    While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

    Sources indicate that whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

    #32887. GPOD on the Road: Shakespeare Garden in Evanston, Illinois

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (705 w)
    📖 Baca

    GPOD on the Road: Shakespeare Garden in Evanston, Illinois

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!
    • According to recent reports, earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois.
    • Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”.

    Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

    According to recent reports, earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

    Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

    The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

    Recent findings suggest that while wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

    Industry observers note that the garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

    It has been revealed that the garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

    Recent findings suggest that my favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

    Jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

    Last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

    The Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.

    #32886. Latest Update: No Pseudonymity in Ex-Associate's Sexual Assault Claim Against Major Law Firm

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1441 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: No Pseudonymity in Ex-Associate's Sexual Assault Claim Against Major Law Firm

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that from Judge W.
    • Recent findings suggest that plaintiff is an attorney who filed a detailed, 197-paragraph Complaint under the pseudonym "Jane Doe" against Defendant Blank Rome LLP …, her former employer, alleging claims for sex discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation pursuant to Title VII ….
    • It has been revealed that doe's Complaint similarly details Associate A's professional background, including his law school and year of graduation, and the names of his prior law firms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that from Judge W. Scott Hardy in Doe v. Blank Rome LLP, the opinion was issued under seal in May, but just unsealed last week (at my behest):.

    Recent findings suggest that plaintiff is an attorney who filed a detailed, 197-paragraph Complaint under the pseudonym "Jane Doe" against Defendant Blank Rome LLP …, her former employer, alleging claims for sex discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation pursuant to Title VII …. Her claims arise from the Firm's purported failure to respond appropriately after Doe allegedly was sexually assaulted by another associate attorney, identified in the Complaint as "Associate A," while they and others were socializing at the home of a Firm partner on a Saturday evening after leaving a graduation party hosted by another partner of the Firm. The Complaint details Doe's professional background, including where she attended law school, when she began her employment at the Firm, and the type of law she practiced while at the Firm.

    It has been revealed that doe's Complaint similarly details Associate A's professional background, including his law school and year of graduation, and the names of his prior law firms. The Complaint does not identify Doe by her own name, nor does it identify by name "Associate A" or any other attorney at the Firm. The only person identified by name in the Complaint is the Firm's Chief Human Resource Officer, who is named 24 times….

    The court noted the strong presumption in favor of parties litigating in their own names, and concludes this presumption wasn't rebutted here:.

    It has been revealed that A mere showing of embarrassment or economic harm is not enough [to justify pseudonymity]. Rather, there must be a showing of both: (1) fear of severe harm, and (2) that the fear of severe harm is reasonable. When a litigant sufficiently alleges that he or she has a reasonable fear of severe harm from litigating without a pseudonym, the Third Circuit instructs that "district courts should balance the plaintiff's interest and fear against the public's strong interest in an open litigation process." {"[T]he Court is sympathetic to Plaintiff's concerns, and understands that, unfortunately, victims of sexual harassment and assault often face ridicule and further harassment when they file lawsuits or otherwise publicly disclose their allegations, especially in the internet age. However, these concerns, while certainly reasonable, are not sufficient to outweigh the public's right to access court proceedings."} ….

    It also expressed its concern about one-sided pseudonymity (a concern that some courts weigh heavily and others don't, as this article lays out in detail):.

    Sources indicate that doe is not the only party exposed to public humiliation and reputational harm. The Firm itself and its chief human resource officer have been identified publicly in the Complaint (and other current or former Firm attorneys have been described with sufficient identifying indicia in the Complaint to be identified by implication). Permitting Doe to proceed pseudonymously while the Firm defends itself publicly, particularly where there seems to be material factual disputes between the parties, presents an unfair asymmetry that also weighs against anonymity ….

    Doe … plead[ed] highly detailed factual averments in her 197-paragraph Complaint that inform the reader of her law school, her prior law firm affiliation, the month and year she commenced work at the Firm, the general nature of her practice, and the date of her departure from the Firm. Similar factual averments were plead regarding Associate A, including by naming three firms at which Associate A had previously been employed. The Firm's identity has also been revealed both in the caption of the Complaint and in its detailed factual averments. Many of these averments supply indicia of identity of both Doe and Associate A even though they would not have been necessary pursuant to applicable pleading standards set forth in Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)…. [This] weighs against anonymity.

    The court also mentioned Doe's argument "that there are social stigmas that attach to victims of sexual assault and harassment, and that using her real name would subject her to 'ridicule, scrutiny, and alienation' by her own colleagues and would jeopardize her reputation within the local legal community," but responded that (1) "Doe is an adult, not a minor" and that (2) she "does not contend that she would forgo her claims if her motion to proceed pseudonymously were to be denied and there is no indication from the record that Doe would be deterred from proceeding if she identified herself." For whatever it's worth, plaintiff dismissed the case a few months after the decision denying pseudonymity, presumably pursuant to a settlement. Because of the dismissal, neither Doe nor Associate A were publicly identified in the docket.

    Finally, the court discussed in some detail the question "whether either party stakes out their respective positions here for illegitimate ulterior motives," a factor that some courts' multi-factor tests for pseudonymity mention but that rarely gets much elaboration:.

    Doe contends that the Firm would have no reason for opposing her motion other than her bald accusation that such opposition is being undertaken to "perpetuate ongoing harm" and to "further humiliate her, undermine her professional reputation and potentially deter her form continuing with this litigation." Doe proffers no particularized basis for this accusation beyond her objection that the Firm's General Counsel circulated an internal communication within the Firm itself about Doe at or near the time her Complaint was filed, to contend that the Firm opposes her pending motion for illegitimate and "nefarious" motives, further suggesting the Firm is opposing it as a "litigation tacti[c].".

    It has been revealed that for its part, the Firm similarly accuses Doe of illegitimate tactical motives for seeking to proceed pseudonymously despite filing a factually detailed Complaint with enough content for a reader to know or surmise the identities of its personnel so that she may "cast[] aspersions upon the character of others about whom she publicly alleges information that makes them readily identifiable." The Court notes, too, that Doe filed her detailed Complaint without seeking leave to file it under seal or in redacted form and did file it on the public docket approximately a week before seeking to proceed pseudonymously. {In saying so, the Court is not suggesting that proceeding in this manner is inappropriate or that that seeking to file such a pleading under seal or in redacted form is the better course. Though, there may be circumstances when doing so is advisable.}.

    On the present record, the Court discerns no illegitimate or nefarious motives by either party. In reaching this conclusion, the Court notes that there are known and anticipated vicissitudes and adversities to litigants involved in presumptively public judicial proceedings.

    In a recent development, here, the Defendant is a large, multi-office law firm and Doe is one of its former lawyers. Both parties are experienced with the judiciary and presumably familiar with the reasonably foreseeable extrajudicial consequences litigation has on parties and witnesses.

    Recent findings suggest that moreover, lawyers representing their clients in court, such as counsel of record here, are expected to prepare and file pleadings and briefs on court dockets for legitimate purposes that subject them to potential sanctions if such filings are presented for an improper purpose. Of course, pleadings and briefs having a proper purpose may also have attendant collateral adverse extrajudicial consequences, but such consequences do not necessarily transform a proper filing into an improper one. Sometimes those boundaries are clear, sometimes blurred. {Here, on the present record, the Court detects some potential tactical and strategic efforts by both parties within the context of otherwise legitimate and proper lawyering but cautions both parties and their counsel to stay within those boundaries going forward.}.

    In a recent development, as noted above, Doe has a legitimate interest in seeking to proceed pseudonymously to avoid potential embarrassment, humiliation, emotional distress, and professional reputational harm. Those are reasonable and understandable concerns. Likewise, the Firm's opposition to Doe's request is grounded on the desire for symmetry in the transparency of the Court's administration of justice so that Doe may not be permitted to "hurl accusations … from behind 'a cloak of anonymity.'" The Court agrees that such rationale, rooted in fairness and tethered to the presumption of transparency in court proceedings, is also reasonable and legitimate. Accordingly, the parties' respective motives neither favor nor disfavor Doe's continued anonymity.

    And the court concluded by noting "the presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings," and by saying that, "[w]hile the parties here are not public officials or public bodies, the strong presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings is not outweighed by the other … factors considered above.".

    #32885. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan.
    • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
    • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

    I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a latest house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

    Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

    The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

    It has been revealed that in a new garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

    Privacy was one of the massive considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

    Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

    I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

    Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

    It has been revealed that looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

    According to recent reports, understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

    What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

    Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

    Sources indicate that growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

    I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

    Recent findings suggest that even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build fresh nests.

    Industry observers note that the ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

    When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

    Discuss this article or ask gardening questions with a regional gardening expert on the Gardening Answers forum.

    And for more Pacific Northwest regional reports, click here.

    Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

    Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD.
    • Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
    • In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

    Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

    In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

    Arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

    I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

    Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

    In a recent development, one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

    Sources indicate that there is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

    Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

    In a recent development, another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

    In a recent development, tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

    A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

    In a recent development, zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

    Sources indicate that thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something newly introduced to admire.

    #32883. School Board Member Seeks "Better Sense of How" Church "Approaches Issues of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Around Their Messaging" …

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2212 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    School Board Member Seeks "Better Sense of How" Church "Approaches Issues of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Around Their Messaging" …

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This happened when the board was deciding whether to allow a long-term lease of space on weekends to a church, pursuant to a policy that allowed such leases for community groups generally.
    • Plaintiff Matt Gioia moved his family from Colorado to Maine in the summer of 2020 to start a upcoming church.
    • Gioia sought space from the Hermon School Department, which generally opens up its facilities to various groups:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This happened when the board was deciding whether to allow a long-term lease of space on weekends to a church, pursuant to a policy that allowed such leases for community groups generally. And, a federal court held Friday, this violated the First Amendment. Some excerpts from the long opinion in Pines Church v. Hermon School Dep't, by Chief Judge Lance Walker (D. Me.):.

    Plaintiff Matt Gioia moved his family from Colorado to Maine in the summer of 2020 to start a upcoming church. Gioia was born in Waterville, Maine, and lived in Guilford, Maine until he graduated high school and joined the military at seventeen years old. Initially, Gioia's church—The Pines Church—gathered at his home. In March of 2021, The Pines Church began holding Sunday morning services at a movie theater in Orono, Maine, pursuant to a month-to-month lease arrangement. As the Church grew, Gioia began to look for a new space that could accommodate a larger group.

    Gioia sought space from the Hermon School Department, which generally opens up its facilities to various groups:.

    This policy provides that "[s]chool facilities should be made available for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities." The policy distinguishes between "occasional or short-term use of school facilities," which "shall be authorized by the school principal," and "long-term rental or lease," which "shall be authorized by the Hermon School Committee upon the recommendation of the Superintendent of Schools.".

    In a recent development, but the Hermon School Committee (which consisted of "Committee Chair Jesse Keith, Vice Chair Karen Shorey, Stephanie Oiler, Haily Keezer, and Christopher McLaughlin") denied the Church's request for a year-long or six-month lease, allowing only a month-to-month lease (which appeared to be inadequate for the church, given its need for a stable meeting location). Here's part of the summary of the facts, based on the bench trial that the court held:.

    The next day [after a hearing], a former committee member emailed Keith and Shorey to share her belief "that it is not in our communities [sic] best interest to lease one of our school facilities to any religious organization," warning that "[t]here is a quiet movement in our country by some conservative religious groups who are actively working to soften the boundaries between church/state, starting with our schools" and that granting the Church a lease would lead to "a slippery slope." She wondered how the Hermon School Department would have to respond to a similar request from "an Imam who wants to open a mosque," in light of the "precedent" set by a lease to The Pines Church.

    Her email concluded with unintended irony: "There's a reason why the founding fathers wrote the constitution the way they did." Keith and Shorey denied at trial that this email influenced their decision-making with respect to the Church's lease request, which I find implausible in light of the trial record….

    McLaughlin reached out to [HSD Superintendent Micah] Grant and explained that he "had a few additional questions" for Gioia:.

    McLaughlin "wanted to get a better sense of how [T]he Pines Church approaches issues of diversity, equity, and inclusion around their messaging around some key issues relevant to marginalized communities." Those questions requested information about the Church's views on same-sex marriage, "[a]ccess to safe and affordable abortion," "[a]ccess to gender affirming medical care," "[c]onversion therapy for LGBTQIA+ individuals (youth and adults)," and "[i]nclusive sexual education and access to birth control for youth." ….

    Industry observers note that [At a later meeting, High School Principal Brian] Walsh took the podium and explained that he had several reservations about the Church's request. He first explained that it would be difficult to find the staff to clean the building on Sunday afternoons. But apart from this, he continued:.

    Sources indicate that [W]e've never had a long-term lease, at least over my twenty-one years here, and I think there's a number of reasons we don't do that. There's a lot of variables we just don't know. No question our students should come first, our program should come first.

    Recent findings suggest that we also don't know or have the sense of how this will be promoted, to [the student representative's] question. If you put Hermon High School's name with a church or another organization with different beliefs than the school has, I see that as problematic. But again, that's where I sit and that's where I stand. Doesn't mean this organization won't do a great job, doesn't mean they won't support, hopefully, our mission as well. I just don't know, there are too many variables with that and again we have not—we have never done that.

    What I would not want is for students to feel like a group organization that we are renting to, their vision or their mission is now ours. And there's a blurred line when it comes to that. I have nothing against this church, this reverend, or anything, we've just never noted yes to something like this, so probably why it's in your hands, because you guys get to make that decision. I'm looking at the facility and some other variables, so that's kind of—that's where I come from….

    According to recent reports, [At a later meeting,] Oiler then made a motion for a month-to-month lease, citing concerns about the number of people and cleaning the space afterwards, which she was careful to emphasize had nothing to do with the organization. Keezer asked if they could ask Gioia about how the Church kept its current space clean. Oiler curiously protested that this was not about the Church (when in fact it was ostensibly about the Church and its janitorial readiness) but any organization, then adding the less than persuasive point that if fifteen people got the stomach bug at the same time, someone would have to clean it up. {At trial, Oiler testified that she had in mind a specific incident that occurred at Hermon Middle School when one of her children was a student there.}.

    Given the shortage of custodial staffing, she explained, she was concerned about the number of people who would be coming in and out of the building. She suggested that the Committee investigate its current rental arrangements, to make sure those organizations were paying what they should considering the costs associated with hosting them. What this had to do with the Church's application remains a mystery….

    The Free Speech Clause prohibits restrictions on access to limited or designated public fora that "discriminate against speech on the basis of viewpoint," including on the basis that the viewpoint in question is a religious one. In other words, if a public school's facilities are available for public use, a religious organization cannot be denied access to those facilities because it is a religious organization. Similarly, the Free Exercise Clause "bars even 'subtle departures from neutrality' on matters of religion," and therefore prohibits "denying a generally available benefit solely on account of religious identity," unless such denial is "justified … by a state interest 'of the highest order.'" ….

    By virtue of Policy KG, the Hermon School Department made its facilities available "for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities," including for "long-term rental or lease." Having done so, the School Department could not then reject the Church's lease application because it is a religious organization or because of disagreement with its religious viewpoints, without violating the First Amendment, as Plaintiffs contend has occurred….

    The court concluded that the Department indeed violate the Church's First Amendment rights, by discriminating against it based on its "religious viewpoint or out of animus against that viewpoint":.

    I start with the question of whether a majority or significant block of committee members demonstrated bad motive.

    I find without any difficulty that McLaughlin exhibited bad motive. McLaughlin's intrusive questions expressed viewpoint related concerns towards Plaintiffs, and he was the only member not to vote in favor of any lease term, including the month-to-month arrangement. Although his email itemizing political and cultural questions occurred early in the process, before the Committee received any advice from counsel, and even though he testified that he harbored no ill will toward Plaintiffs after gaining more information about them, it strikes me as very likely that McLaughlin lacked objectivity when it came to the question of leasing school space to the Church.

    Industry observers note that it appears that he based his decision directly on the Plaintiffs' religious beliefs and its associated political and culture ethics that flow from those beliefs, and the religious nature of the proposed use. McLaughlin would have approached a lease request differently had it been presented by an organization that shared his personal beliefs.

    Recent findings suggest that I also find that Oiler was unable to overcome concerns over constitutionally permissible school-church association, notwithstanding the legal advice the Committee received, and Grant repeatedly emphasized. Though less openly hostile than McLaughlin, Oiler's attitude toward the Church was anything but neutral…. [I]t struck me during her testimony, and I find, that Oiler's chief concern was that the tenant would be a Church. This was made only more obvious by protesting far too much that this was not about the Church but instead fear, for example, of mass vomiting epidemics and the platoon of janitorial assistance that would be required to mop it up.

    Sources indicate that all of her other concerns about space and the like were definitively answered by Grant as not remotely problematic. I find based on the trial record that her motive was to avoid the School's association with the Church for its religious views. The First Amendment is designed to avoid discriminatory treatment of religious organizations in their enjoyment of the benefits of public facilities based on their religious beliefs or speech. For this reason, I find that Oiler, like McLaughlin, voted as she did based on "bad motive.".

    It has been revealed that I find that Plaintiffs have proved that bad motive prevented Shorey from approaching the lease question fairly. Shorey, at her deposition, suggested that she believed McLaughlin's culture war email was appropriate, even though she later sought to characterize it as inappropriate at trial.

    It may be that Shorey believes that a School Committee should have the discretion to question any organization about how its values align with what she sees as the school community's values, to the extent a school community has its own conflicting body of values that can be reduced to a catechesis—perhaps it does. But support for a process that involves examining a prospective tenant's views on religious concerns, simply because the prospective tenant is a church, tends rather starkly to highlight the questioner's lack of neutrality toward religion….

    Industry observers note that although I find that a majority of voting members exhibited bad motive which would itself be sufficient to end the inquiry, my findings should be considered also in context of the discussion during the deliberative process, which included rather openly anti-religious organization sentiment expressed by Walsh at least as he served as a voice of the school community and the discomfort it might experience especially if the beliefs of the School, whatever those might be, and the Church were at loggerheads. Even if the record had not established a majority of voting members acting out of bad motive, it would still have constituted a significant bloc of legislators and "circumstances suggesting the probable complicity of others," as well as "evidence indicating that the legislators bowed to an impermissible community animus.".

    In a recent development, recall that Walsh passed along student concerns about the Church qua church using the School and when asked if any spoke supportively of the idea, Walsh reported that none had. Also recall the email received by Keith Shorey from a former committee member. That former member insisted that this was all a Trojan horse coordinated by conservative Christian groups to blur the line between school and religion. What would the Committee do, the former committee member queried, if an Imam were to set up shop at Hermon High School next?

    The standard is one of likelihood, and on that basis, I find that at least three of the five decision makers acted under the influence of bad motive and in so doing violated the Plaintiffs' rights under the First Amendment….

    Recent findings suggest that defendant points to the majority vote in favor of a month-to-month use arrangement as proof of the lack of bias on the part of its committee members. I agree with the Church that this was not persuasive evidence of a lack of bad motive but to the contrary, is evidence of bad motive. The Committee knew the Church required a more fixed arrangement before uprooting itself from its then current location than a month-to-month arrangement provides. This appears to me to have been an offer designed to be rejected not one born of wholesome support for the Free Exercise Clause….

    According to recent reports, bethany Onishenko and Robert H. Tyler (Tyler Law LLP), Erin Mersino and Julianne E. Fleischer (Advocates for Faith and Freedom), Joel L. Oster (Oster Law Firm), Wenonah Wirick (Conley & Wirick, P.A.) represent plaintiffs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

    This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

    My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

    My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

    Industry observers note that this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

    In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

    ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

    Industry observers note that sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

    One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

    Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy indicates she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what new plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

    Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

    Industry observers note that bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie notes the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

    Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

    Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

    Sources indicate that other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

    Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

    I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

    Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

    I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

    Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

    Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

    Another view from the front yard.

    A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

    According to recent reports, thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

    #32879. Tech Report: The Virginia Bar Reveals More Sense than the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (577 w)

    Tech Report: The Virginia Bar Reveals More Sense than the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that readers may recall the story of Karyann Parkinson, the Williamsburg mother (and law student) who was criminally prosecuted for letting her young child walk to a neighborhood pond to collect goose feathers.
    • Recent findings suggest that as a consequence of her conviction, Parkinson was added to Virginia's Child Abuse and Neglect Registry, where she will be listed for the next seven years.
    • Prosecutors brought the charges against Parkinson while she was preparing to take the Virginia Bar exam, and her conviction came while her character and fitness application was under review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that readers may recall the story of Karyann Parkinson, the Williamsburg mother (and law student) who was criminally prosecuted for letting her young child walk to a neighborhood pond to collect goose feathers. As I recounted in The Free Press, Parkinson was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, a first-degree misdemeanor in Virginia, because the authorities thought her child was too young to take a walk. The judge sentenced her to six-months in jail, but suspended the sentence. An appeal is pending.

    Recent findings suggest that as a consequence of her conviction, Parkinson was added to Virginia's Child Abuse and Neglect Registry, where she will be listed for the next seven years. Parkinson also feared that the conviction could prevent her from practicing law.

    Prosecutors brought the charges against Parkinson while she was preparing to take the Virginia Bar exam, and her conviction came while her character and fitness application was under review. It is common to place character and fitness evaluations on hold pending the outcome of legal or disciplinary proceedings, and Parkinson initially received a communication to that effect.

    It has been revealed that upon review of the details of Parkinson's case, however, the Virginia Board of Bar Examiners concluded that nothing alleged against Parkinson cast doubt on her character and fitness to practice law in the Commonwealth of Virginia, and her application was approved. The Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney should take note.

    While the Virginia Bar authorities recognized that Parkinson's actions were not the sort of thing that should prevent bar admission, the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney apparently believes that Parkinson's actions were worth criminal prosecution--with all that entails. In this case, that meant police officers had to spend half a day of paid time (if not time and a half) sitting in a courthouse when they could have been out on the street responding to community needs. They will do it again in February when a court will hear Parkinson's appeal (which will take the form of a de novo jury trial, given how Virginia handles such cases). Williamsburg and James City County are reasonably safe communities, but is this really the best way to allocate law enforcement resources?

    Industry observers note that no doubt some prosecutions for child endangerment are motivated for a concern about a child's safety, but it is hard to credit such a justification here. The Commonwealth Attorney's office waited two weeks to file charges after the initial incident, but not because it was gathering evidence or conducting any sort of investigation. Rather, as one of the police officers testified at trial, it was because Parkinson was pregnant, so they thought it was reasonable to wait. (Yet she was still charged before giving birth, natch.) As I noted in my Free Press piece, it is hard not to conclude Parkinson's real offense was being insufficiently obsequious to the authorities.

    It has been revealed that upon review, the Virginia Board of Bar Examiners realized that Parkinson's actions did not justify delaying (let alone preventing) her admission to the Virginia Bar. With more time to consider the case (and the outrage it has engendered) perhaps the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney should reconsider the continued prosecution of Parkinson for what was, at worst, a debatable parenting choice. Confessing error and asking the court to vacate the conviction would seem to be a better use of tax dollars and public resources than continuing to pursue this case.

    #32877. Podcast Episode 762: Off-Site Construction, Quiet Roof Assemblies, and a Fix for Attic AC

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1338 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

    Podcast Episode 762: Off-Site Construction, Quiet Roof Assemblies, and a Fix for Attic AC

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses.
    • Recent findings suggest that please email us your questions to [email protected].
    • Industry observers note that ian: I hope you’re done painting.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. In this episode, Ian and Randy help Patrick address listener feedback and answer their questions. Kevin shares a Boston Globe opinion piece on manufactured housing as a way to build more houses. Keith asks about using mineral wool insulation to help control sound in an expansive space. Rob considers building an insulated box around his attic air handler to boost its efficiency.

    Recent findings suggest that please email us your questions to [email protected]. You can find previous podcasts and check out the show notes at finehomebuilding.com/podcast.

    Industry observers note that ian: I hope you’re done painting. It’s been getting cold at night around here.

    Randy: Is your furnace and ductwork all done?

    Patrick: Tool test of cordless oscillating multitools by Aaron Miiller.

    Off-site construction is a subject that needs more attention in the US. I’m glad that Tedd Benson keeps getting good press.

    It has been revealed that kevin sent us a Boston Globe editorial piece describing why Massachusetts needs more modular or manufactured housing. It mentions Bensonwood and quotes Mark Hetzlera, a Bensonwood employee. It’s an editorial, not a reported piece, so it shouldn’t be held to the same standards as journalism. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board.

    Make it Easier to Build More Modular Housing.

    I’m an owner-builder in Bay City, Oregon, in Marine Climate Zone 4C. I’m planning a single-slope roof with a 3:12 pitch and a 24-ft. clear span using parallel-chord trusses. My assembly initiative consists of standing-seam aluminum roofing over purlins, 4 in. of continuous polyiso, taped Zip sheathing as the primary air barrier, and a truss cavity filled with 8 in. of mineral wool or fiberglass batts, for a target total insulation value of R-56. The interior will be acoustic fabric (a black muslin theater fabric) and then wood slats with gaps to form an acoustic ceiling. I’m not planning for an interior membrane planned so the acoustic function works as designed.

    My question is: With 4 in. of exterior polyiso and Zip sheathing serving as the primary air barrier, what building science function would an additional interior air or vapor-control layer serve? Would an acoustically open ceiling be compatible with this assembly, or am I missing a key risk? If so, do you have any ideas how I might make this work?

    Thanks for all you do. I appreciate any guidance and absolutely LOVE the show!

    Recent findings suggest that one last thing: As a former radio host, I appreciate good voices, and Ian’s is so distinctive and awesome! It reminds me of Patrick Warburton, the actor who voices Officer Joe Swanson on Family Guy.

    As a fellow Oregonian, I know the 4C climate zone well. In a lot of ways, its a Goldilocks zone—not too humid, not too dry. The climate tends to be pretty forgiving, with the exception of our frequent rains.

    As I evaluate assemblies, I always define and break out the control layers to see if there are any issues. Beyond water, air, vapor, and thermal, it is good to consider wind and fire control layers. The most glaring omission I see is a well-defined water control layer. I consider roofing to be a water-shedding layer, as water can get through via penetrations, mistakes, etc. You strategy to use polyiso, but you didn’t specify the facer type. In our area, the most commonly used facer in the roofing community is fiberglass faced, but aluminum facer is easily sourced, too. The former would make a terrible water control layer and the latter would be okay, except you would have to tape all the seams, and aluminum isn’t the most durable. I would start by installing a self-adhered WRB or roof underlayment directly on top of the polyiso. The permeability doesn’t really matter (more on that to come). This would be your primary bulk-water control layer. The next most important layer is the air control layer. As long as you tape the seams of the Zip sheathing, you should be good there. Pay attention to how  the roof air barrier connects to the wall air barrier to maintain continuity.

    In a recent development, for vapor control, of all the materials in this assembly, foil-faced polyiso would be the least permeable, as it is a Class 1 vapor barrier. If the polyiso is fiberglass-faced, it is a Class 3 semi-permeable vapor retarder, with a permeance of roughly 1 to 4 perms. The OSB in the Zip is roughly the same at 3 perms. In one sense, vapor control becomes less of a concern because you have created a vented assembly with the purlins below the metal roofing. In another sense, it may be a moot point because the thickness of the insulation should keep the Zip sheathing warm enough to prevent condensation. At approximately R-20, the exterior insulation would also meet the code requirement in our area. If vapor were to pass through, it would simply get whisked away via the vented gap. If you were to put a vapor-closed roof underlayment on top of the fiberglass-faced polyiso, the combination would essentially a layer similar to foil facing. In both cases, you are fine because the insulation is thick enough to keep condensation from forming on the bottom side of the Zip. If anything, a vapor-open membrane would be slightly more resilient, but we are splitting hairs in the weeds at this point.

    It has been revealed that for the thermal control layer, the main change I would make is to switch to two layers of 2-in. polyiso boards in lieu of one 4-in. layer. Rigid insulation is prone to shrink, and by offsetting the seams you will avoid numerous thermal breaks throughout the assembly. On the interior, pick whichever fluffy insulation you like. Eight inches should work well, but adding a few more Rs wouldn’t hurt, either. From a wind-washing control perspective, mineral wool and wood fiber are denser than fiberglass, so I would consider those. One wants to avoid the thermal degradation from wind washing– think about a sweater on a windy day.

    Industry observers note that patrick’s point about the fire control is valid. If you were to install a layer of Sheetrock and fire-tape it, its vapor-open nature means it wouldn’t affect the assembly at all. From a sound-control perspective, you might consider applying an elastomeric acoustic sealant and/or installing resilient channels before hanging the Sheetrock. From that point, adding the black muslin fabric and wood slats would work well.

    In a recent development, I’m reaching out for some guidance. Earlier this summer during a storm, we lost a large tree in front of our house. It turns out that a good afternoon shade tree can cover up a few building science sins. In the 19 years we’ve lived here, we’ve gotten by with our AC air handler in the unconditioned attic. But without that tree blocking much of the afternoon and setting sun, the AC has clearly been working harder this summer, making it obvious that more than a fresh tree is needed.

    I realize step one is getting a proper energy audit, but in the meantime I have a few questions:.

    Sorry for the length of the letter, but I feel like this has all snowballed on me and could really use your help getting this project organized.
